title: How bad does a polluted night in London look in our health data? | Terra
summary: On the most polluted nights, sleeping heart rate rose 1.4 bpm, heart-rate variability fell, and people took fewer steps.
body_markdown:
## Same person, dirtier night


I kept anyone with at least 13 outdoor workouts inside Greater London between 9 August and 9 November. About one a week. The data are anonymised, so there is no home address. Where someone is, approximately, comes from the workout, and I line that up with the night. That is an assumption, but a fairly safe one.


The sleeping-heart-rate model is 2,237 people and 106,461 nights.


Everything is within the person. I am not comparing a Londoner to a New Yorker. I am comparing someone's Saturday in August with their Saturday in November, after taking out temperature, wind, the day of the week, and how long they trained that day. A cold, still night raises pollution and it can move heart rate on its own. I did not want to give the particles credit for the weather.


What moved Per +10 µg/m³ 95% CI People


Sleeping heart rate +0.20 bpm +0.16 to +0.24 2,237


Resting heart rate, overnight +0.15 bpm +0.09 to +0.21 1,604


Resting heart rate, across the day +0.23 bpm +0.18 to +0.28 2,872


HRV, rMSSD −0.7% −1.2% to −0.2% 866


HRV, SDNN −0.4% −0.7% to −0.1% 782


Steps −112 −147 to −77 3,240


Time asleep −0.7 min −1.1 to −0.2 2,212


Breathing rate +0.007 /min includes zero 2,136


Sleeping heart rate on that single slope is +0.20 bpm per 10 µg/m³. Minimum heart rate moved with it, +0.18. On the Friday-to-Sunday nights above 40 µg/m³, compared with the same people's other Friday-to-Sunday nights under 12, sleeping heart rate was 1.4 bpm higher (64.7 against 63.3, 892 people).


## The line bends


***Figure 3. Sleeping heart rate against how dirty the night was.** Difference from the same person's average, after temperature, wind, weekday and that day's exercise. The vertical line is the 95% interval. The last three points are a handful of nights.*


Below 30 µg/m³, which is all but three of the nights, sleeping heart rate rises about +0.46 bpm per 10. Above 30 the extra slope is about zero, and with only those three nights I cannot tell it from zero. A night around 4 sits 0.12 bpm under that person's own average. A night around 30 sits 0.64 above it. The polluted nights, the ones around 78, sit 0.76 above. So last Saturday is not a new step up from a moderately polluted night. Most of it has already happened by the time the air is in the high 20s. The interval is narrow on the clean nights because that is where almost all the data sit. The higher nights are few, thankfully. With more of them, that top end could move.


Leave 5–8 November out and the single slope goes from +0.20 to +0.51 bpm per 10, because what you have left is the steep bit. rMSSD goes from −0.7% to −1.2%, and SDNN from −0.4% to −2.1%, which is similar to the published literature.


I use steps as a decent bellwether for whether people went out. 112 fewer steps per 10 µg/m³ of that day's PM2.5. On a day that is 50 above a normal one, that is about 500 fewer steps. People went out less. I did not look at whether the runs that still happened were harder. Pace-adjusted heart rate is a different question, and a messier one, as we've discussed in previous posts.


Time asleep also moved, but I trust it less. 0.7 minutes shorter per 10, and about 5 minutes shorter on the offending weekend. Drop 5–8 November and the duration effect goes away. Those nights were fireworks, fog and a weekend. People stay up. Breathing rate never cleared the noise.


## Is it just London in November?


I ran the same comparison for three months in eight other cities, same rule of about one outdoor workout a week. The pollution number outside London is a model (CAMS, via Open-Meteo), not a street monitor, so I trust the London slope more than these. The point was to see if the pattern was a one-weekend fluke.


Figure 4 is the same heart-rate slope against a usual overnight PM2.5. Cleaner cities sit on the left. The slope gets smaller as that usual night gets higher.


***Figure 4. Sleeping heart rate per +10 µg/m³ against a usual overnight PM2.5.** The vertical line is the 95% interval. London is measured by street monitors. The other cities are from an Open-Meteo model, not direct measurements.*


The cities near zero are the ones whose usual night is already high, up where London's own curve flattens. Los Angeles, usual night 22, slope about zero. Seoul, 22, flat. Mexico City, 24, flat. Delhi, where a typical night was already 82 and the peak was 175, was +0.10 in 40 people. This makes sense. It is what you would expect if another 10 barely matters once you are already living with that pollution.


Paris has similarly clean air, a usual night of 7, and the slope was the steep one: +0.40 bpm per 10 (230 people). Resting heart rate there was +0.72. Milan still rises, +0.25 in only 41 people. Its usual night is 19, but the cleaner nights still drop to around 9, so much of the contrast is in the steep part.


Madrid and Mexico City did not show a clear heart-rate rise. They did show fewer steps, −566 and −258 per 10.


New York is the one that does not fit with the trend, and it is the biggest sample I have. A usual night there is 14, and the clean nights are about 5, so it covers the same range where London's heart rate rises. Steps fell, −203 per 10 (5,505 people). Sleeping heart rate did not rise. It was 0.06 bpm lower, in 3,658 people. I am not going to explain that away. Over this autumn, on a model rather than street monitors, New York does not reproduce the London heart-rate result.


## What I think it means


A more polluted night comes with a higher sleeping heart rate and lower heart-rate variability. Fewer steps happen on a dirtier day. The heart-rate rise mostly comes from the step from a clean night to a moderately dirty one. London's usual night is 5. The weekend got to 94, but the data seem to show the biggest change when pollution was registering in the high 20s. That top end only has a handful of nights to go on, so this could change if we had more data. The people who slept through both the polluted Friday-to-Sunday and a clean one were about a beat and a half higher on the polluted one.


It is an association. The monitors are in specific places, not outside your bedroom window, and the air indoors will have been cleaner than the kerb. The subjects train, and they own a wearable. Within those limits, the data produced a sizeable result. Pollution shows up as a measurable shift in the physiology.
